crust: the thin, hard outer shell of the Earth
mantle: the thick layer of hot, slow-flowing rock below the crust
core: the ball of very hot metal at the centre of the Earth
plate: one of the giant moving pieces of the Earth's crust
volcano: a place where molten rock bursts out of the ground
erosion: the slow wearing away of land by water, wind or ice

Our Earth has not always looked as it does. If you could travel back four and a half thousand million years, you would find no seas, no green land, no living thing at all. The young Earth was a spinning ball of molten rock, glowing red hot, crashed into again and again by lumps of rock from space. It was a world of fire.

image.note: The newborn Earth, a red-hot molten globe, meteors striking it; fierce, primal

pages.text: Slowly, over millions of years, the surface cooled and hardened into a thin crust of rock, the way hot soup grows a skin as it cools. This thin, hard shell is the ground you stand on today. But do not be fooled by how solid it feels. Beneath it, the Earth is still fiercely hot, even now.

image.note: The Earth's surface hardening into a dark crust over the still-glowing interior; cooling

pages.text: As the young Earth cooled, steam that had poured out of it gathered into thick clouds, and rain began to fall. It rained, by some accounts, for an unimaginably long time, and the water gathered in the low places until the great oceans were formed. The blue that covers most of our world was born from that long, ancient rain.

image.note: Endless rain falling on a young dark Earth, water pooling into the first oceans; moody, epic

pages.text: The air changed too. At first it was nothing you could have breathed. But once tiny life appeared in the oceans, some of it began to give off a gas we cannot live without: oxygen. Over vast ages, these tiny living things filled the sky with the very air you are breathing right now. Life itself made the world fit to live on.

image.note: Tiny sea life releasing bubbles that rise and fill the sky with breathable air; time-lapse feel

pages.text: What lies beneath your feet? If you could cut the Earth open like a fruit, you would find it built in layers. On the outside is the thin, hard crust. Below that lies a thick layer of hot, slow-flowing rock called the mantle. And right at the centre is the core, a ball of metal hotter than the surface of the Sun.

image.note: A clean cutaway of the Earth showing crust, mantle and glowing metal core; labelled, clear

pages.text: The thin crust you live on is not one solid shell. It is cracked into enormous pieces, like the cracked shell of a boiled egg. These giant pieces are called plates, and they float on the hot, slow-flowing rock beneath. And here is the astonishing part: these plates are moving, all the time, though far too slowly to feel.

image.note: The Earth's crust shown as great cracked plates, like an egg shell, drifting on the mantle

pages.text: The plates move only as fast as your fingernails grow, an inch or two a year. But given millions of years, that adds up to enormous journeys. This is why, long ago, all the land was joined in one great continent, and why it has since drifted apart into the seven continents we know. The map of the world is slowly, endlessly changing.

image.note: A time-lapse of continents drifting from one landmass to their present shapes; motion over ages

pages.text: You can see the evidence yourself. Look at a map of Africa and South America. Notice how the bulge of one seems to fit into the dip of the other, like two pieces of a puzzle. That is no accident. Long ago they were joined, and the slow drift of the plates carried them apart across the widening ocean.

image.note: Africa and South America shown fitting together like puzzle pieces; the coastlines matching

pages.text: When these giant plates push against one another, tremendous things happen. Where two plates shove together, the rock is slowly crumpled and forced upward over ages, and that is how mountains are made. Even the mighty Himalayas were raised this way, pushed slowly higher as two great plates collided.

image.note: Two plates colliding, the ground buckling upward into a mountain range; slow, immense force

pages.text: Sometimes the plates catch and then suddenly slip, and the ground shakes hard: that is an earthquake. And in some places, the fierce heat below finds a way up through a crack, and molten rock bursts out onto the surface: that is a volcano. These are not the Earth misbehaving. They are simply signs that our planet is still alive inside.

image.note: A volcano erupting with glowing rock, ground cracking; powerful but not showing harm to people

chapters.title: The Slow Work of Water and Ice

pages.text: Not all changes are sudden. Some are so slow you could watch for a lifetime and see nothing, yet over ages they reshape the whole world. Rivers, drop by drop, carve deep valleys out of solid rock. The mighty Gurara Falls, that you may have seen, is slowly, patiently cutting the very ground away beneath it.

image.note: A river carving a deep gorge over time; Gurara Falls shown wearing the rock; patient power

pages.text: Wind wears down mountains grain by grain. Ice, in the coldest lands, grinds whole valleys smooth. Given enough time, the softest water can defeat the hardest rock. The mountains that seem so permanent are, in truth, slowly wearing away, even as new ones are slowly rising. Nothing on Earth stands truly still.

image.note: A tall mountain beside a worn old rounded hill; the same mountain, ages apart; erosion

pages.text: So the Earth is not a finished, unchanging place. It is a living, working planet, hot at its heart, its crust forever drifting, its mountains rising and wearing away, its shape slowly changing over ages far longer than any human life. The solid ground beneath you is the top of a story still being told.

image.note: A grand view of the whole living Earth, hints of its inner fire and drifting plates; awe

pages.text: You will never feel the continents move or watch a mountain rise, for these things happen too slowly for a single life. But now you know they are happening, all the time, right beneath your feet. You are standing on a restless, ancient, changing world, and you are lucky enough to live at one small moment of its enormous story.

image.note: A child standing barefoot on the ground, looking down thoughtfully, faint layers of Earth below; closing
